newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds, dollar fall on rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds, dollar fall on rate hike fears.

text.p: Stocks, bonds and the dollar all tumbled Wednesday on renewed fears of an interest rate hike and fresh worries about corporate earnings.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 70.73 points, or 1.09 percent, to 6,402.52 after earlier falling nearly 130 points.

Just last Friday, the index slumped 145 points before recovering to close down 55 points on cautionary comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,122 to 506 on active volume of 494 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The tape looked bad this morning, like the world was coming to an end," said James Cramer, president of Cramer Co.
The stock market got off to a bad start as bond prices fell sharply on speculation that Japanese investors might be losing their appetite for U.S. Treasury securities.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury fell more than 1-3/4 points, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, shot up to 6.63 percent -- its highest since the close of business on Nov. 6 -- vs. 6.49 percent Tuesday.
Recent strength in bond prices had helped fuel the rally in stocks, with the long-term yield slipping below the psychologically important 6.50 percent level.

"The bond market has stopped going lower in terms of yields and that's important for the stock market," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co. A sustained rise in long-term yields could make bonds more attractive than stocks to investors.
The bond market sell-off was sparked by comments from Robert Hormats, a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs International.

In an interview broadcast on Reuters Financial Television, Hormats said he thought the rising U.S. trade imbalance posed a potential threat to dollar-based assets, which in turn could quell Japanese institutional investors' thirst for U.S. Treasury bonds.

Japan's trade surplus with the United States soared 31.3 percent in October to $3.13 billion, according to Japan's Finance Ministry. The huge Japanese trade surpluses with the United States, have been a source of friction.
The dollar fell to 112.96 Japanese yen from 113.37 yen late on Tuesday. It ended at 1.5380 marks, down from 1.5530 marks late on Tuesday.
In commodities trading, lumber prices tumbled as long-term rates jumped, raising fears that higher mortgage rates would hurt the housing industry, one of the biggest users of wood.
Lumber for January delivery fell the $10 daily limit for the second straight day at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, closing at $389.50 for 1,000 board feet.

January crude oil fell $1.04 to $23.38 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange, capping a decline of 9 percent since Friday, as Iraq resumed exports after a U.N. oil-for-food plan took effect, easing an embargo on Baghdad following its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index dropped 53.2 points or 1.3 percent to close at 3,982.5. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 closed 253.74 points or 1.22 percent lower at 20,568.38.
